# kContainerOS

> A zero-dependency, Rust-based mini OS userland for ARM64 containers. One static binary with no libc, no std and no crates is PID 1, a small shell and the core utilities. Init locks the container down before the command starts.

- Site: https://kcos.21no.de/
- Source and README: https://github.com/BackendStack21/kcontaineros
- Licence: MIT, copyright 21no.de
- Platform: linux/arm64 only

## What it is

- `/sbin/init`: PID 1. Forwards signals to the command, reaps zombies, exits with the command's status.
- `/bin/sh`: a small shell for Dockerfile `RUN`/`CMD` and simple scripts. No `if`, loops, functions, globbing, `$(...)`, here-documents, `trap` or `read`; a script that uses them stops with a syntax error before anything runs.
- Utilities: cat chmod chown cp echo env false kill ln ls mkdir mv ps pwd rm sleep touch true uname.
- A sealed build target (`--target sealed`) contains init only: no shell, no utilities, no writable directory.

## The lockdown

Applied by init to itself before it starts the command, enforced by the kernel, inherited by every process:

- `no_new_privs`: setuid binaries and file capabilities grant nothing.
- No capabilities, even under `--privileged`.
- Landlock: programs execute only from `/bin`, `/sbin`, `/usr` and directories named in `KCOS_EXEC`, and those cannot be written to. A program written at run time cannot be started. Symbolic links are not followed when the rules are set up.
- Landlock: of `/dev`, only the standard devices (`null`, `zero`, `full`, `random`, `urandom`, `tty`, `console`, the terminals) and `/dev/shm` can be read, written or controlled with `ioctl`, plus devices named one by one in `KCOS_DEV`. Under `--privileged` the host's disks can be neither read nor written.
- Landlock: root cannot write to `/proc` or `/sys`. It can still read what it owns there.
- seccomp filter: `ptrace`, `process_vm_readv`/`process_vm_writev`, new namespaces, mounts, `bpf`, `io_uring`, `memfd_create` and similar are refused.
- The image runs as `nobody` (65534) and its files are read-only.

## Audit

An end-to-end security audit of version 0.2.0 found no escape and no privilege gain; three documented security claims were false and are fixed in 1.0.0. It was carried out by an AI model, not by an independent party. Summary: https://github.com/BackendStack21/kcontaineros/blob/main/AUDIT.md

## What it does not do

- It is not a guarantee against kernel bugs.
- It does not limit the network or what can be read; set those with the container runtime.
- It does not stop a process mapping bytes into its own memory as code; such code cannot become a new program and stays under the same restrictions.
- Processes of the same user can read and write each other's memory through `/proc/PID/mem` unless the host enables Yama.
- Whoever owns a file can change its permissions, timestamps and `user.*` extended attributes, in program directories too; not its contents.
- On kernels before 6.10 a device that is not named can be opened for neither reading nor writing and still be driven with `ioctl`.
- POSIX message queues (`mq_open`) do not work under init.
- Host directories shared by Docker Desktop (macOS, Windows) cannot be written to under init; use a volume.
- Binaries must be statically linked. There is no package manager.
- `docker exec`, `--entrypoint` and Dockerfile `RUN` steps start outside init and are not under the Landlock rules or the capability drop.
- Not tested on Kubernetes, with user namespaces, or with any AI agent framework.

## Use

```dockerfile
FROM kcontaineros
COPY my-server /usr/local/bin/my-server
CMD ["my-server"]
```

The README has the full details: security notes, a section on containing AI agent tool servers, common questions (including how to get a writable directory), the supported-features table and a comparison with Alpine.
